opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so comparative advantage is a real and important idea, but I think people lean on it in a way that doesn't survive contact with what advanced AI would actually look like.

The classic argument goes: even if one party is better at everything, it still pays to trade, because the more productive party should specialize in what it's *relatively* best at and let the other party do the rest. So even if AI is better than us at every task, there'll always be something left for humans to do.

The problem is that comparative advantage tells you there's *some* trade that's mutually beneficial. It doesn't tell you the wage will be high enough to live on. The wage a human can command is capped by what it costs to get the same work done some other way. If you can spin up another copy of an AI system, or build another robot, for less than the cost of feeding and housing a person, then the human's comparative advantage is real but worth less than subsistence. You're technically still employable in the economist's sense, but not in any sense that matters for your life.

The analogy I find most useful is horses. Horses had a comparative advantage relative to engines for a long time, and in some narrow sense they still do. But once engines got cheap enough, the market-clearing "wage" for a horse fell below the cost of its upkeep, and the horse population collapsed. Nobody repealed the law of comparative advantage; it just stopped protecting them.

The other piece is that comparative advantage assumes the more productive party faces some constraint: limited hours, limited attention, so it has to choose where to spend itself. With humans, that's true. Einstein can't do everything. But AI capacity can be scaled up by building more compute. If the binding constraint becomes chips and energy rather than labor, then the relevant question is whether a human generates more value than the land, energy, and resources it takes to sustain them would generate if they went to machines instead. And eventually I think the honest answer, in pure market terms, is no.

That's what worries me. It's not that the economy stops needing anything from us all at once. It's that our bargaining power, which has historically been the main thing keeping states and institutions somewhat aligned with ordinary people's interests, quietly erodes. And comparative advantage doesn't save us from that.

r001.rationale: The response says a human’s wage may fall below the cost of their upkeep when AI or robots can do the work more cheaply. It does not explain that transaction costs make employing humans unprofitable.

r002.rationale: The response discusses humans losing bargaining power, but does not predict that involving humans in important decisions will be considered irresponsible when machines offer better alternatives.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the comparative advantage argument is one I hear a lot, and I think it's genuinely a good argument in a narrow sense, but people draw the wrong conclusion from it. The argument goes: even if AIs are better than humans at everything, there's still an opportunity cost to using an AI on any given task, so it will always make sense to let humans do the things where they're relatively least bad. And that's true as far as it goes. Trade can still be mutually beneficial even when one party dominates on every dimension.

But the thing comparative advantage doesn't tell you is anything about the wage. It says there's some positive price at which it's worth employing you. It doesn't say that price covers the cost of keeping you alive, or housed, or that it's anything you'd recognize as a decent living. Think about horses in 1900 versus 1950. Horses never lost their comparative advantage at anything in principle. There was still some task where a horse was relatively least bad compared to a tractor. The problem was that the value of that task fell below the cost of feeding the horse, and so the horse population just collapsed. Nobody passed a law. It just stopped making sense.

The second piece is that the standard argument implicitly assumes the AI is a scarce resource, like a trading partner with a fixed amount of time. But compute isn't like that. If the marginal cost of spinning up another instance of a system that can do your job is a few cents an hour of electricity, then the opportunity cost of using an AI on your task isn't that some other important thing goes undone. It's basically that you have to buy a bit more compute. So the thing you'd be competing against isn't one very talented person with limited hours, it's an arbitrarily replicable worker whose price keeps falling. In that regime your wage gets pinned to roughly the cost of the compute that replaces you, and that's a number that keeps going down.

And I'd add one more thing, which is about what humans actually need in order to work. We need to be fed, trained for twenty years, we get sick, we need motivation, we can only run one copy at a time. All of those are fixed costs that a machine competitor doesn't carry. So even in the world where humans retain a theoretical niche, the niche has to pay for all of that overhead, and I just don't see why it would.

So my honest view is: comparative advantage gives you a reason to think there'll still be transactions involving humans. It gives you no reason at all to think those transactions will support a human economy. That's the gap people are stepping over.

r001.rationale: The response says human wages may not cover the cost of keeping people alive, housed, trained, and motivated. It does not explain that transaction costs make employment unprofitable.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict that involving humans in important decisions will be regarded as irresponsible when machines offer better alternatives.

astra-6.text:
Comparative advantage tells you that two parties can benefit from trading even if one is better at everything. But it doesn’t tell you that the wage a human can earn will be enough to live on.

Usually, the intuition is that a very productive person still has limited time. A surgeon might hire someone to clean their house because doing it themselves means giving up valuable surgery time. But if you can make more copies of an AI, you don’t necessarily have that tradeoff. You can have a copy doing surgery and another copy cleaning the house. The question becomes whether a human can do the work more cheaply than the resources needed to run that extra copy.

There will still be constraints on compute and energy, and there might be jobs where people specifically want another human. So this isn’t a claim that literally no human will ever receive money for doing something. It’s that comparative advantage doesn’t guarantee substantial demand for human labour, or a decent income from it. You can have a much richer economy overall while people who only have their labour to sell lose their bargaining power.

r001.rationale: It explains that AI copies can perform multiple tasks without the human time tradeoff, and compares human labor costs with the resources to run another copy. It does not mention transaction costs as the reason employing humans may be unprofitable.

r002.rationale: It mentions that some people may specifically want another human, but does not predict that involving humans in important decisions will be regarded as irresponsible when machines offer better alternatives.

sol-6.1.text:
Comparative advantage tells you that there can be gains from trade even when one party is better at everything. But it doesn’t guarantee that the wage you can earn will be enough to live on. You might have a comparative advantage at some task, and yet the value of doing that task could be pennies a day.

And there’s another assumption here that matters: the supply of the more capable workers is limited. If someone is much better than me at both programming and gardening, I might still do their gardening because their time is better spent programming. But if they can cheaply make another copy of themselves, they don’t have to choose. They can have one copy program and another garden. Then the relevant question is whether I can do either job more cheaply than an additional copy of the AI.

There could still be things people pay a premium to have a human do. But that’s a much narrower claim than saying comparative advantage guarantees valuable employment for everyone. The economy could become enormously productive while the market value of human labour falls below what people need to support themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says comparative advantage may leave human wages too low to live on and compares human labor costs with AI copies, but it does not explain that transaction costs make employing humans unprofitable.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss human involvement in important decisions or argue that doing so would be considered irresponsible when machines offer better alternatives.
